subtopic_detail: A rapidly growing red lesion on the upper eyelid of a three month old that partly closes the eye when she is tired
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a three month old girl whose parents are worried about a mark on her left upper eyelid. It was a faint pink patch at two weeks of age that they were told would fade, and it has been growing steadily since.

It is now a bright red raised lesion measuring 22 mm across the upper lid. Her mother has photographs on her phone showing it has roughly doubled in size in the past six weeks. By the end of the day, when the child is tired, the lesion droops enough that the upper lid covers the top half of the pupil, and her parents have noticed she prefers to look to the right. The lesion is soft, compressible, not ulcerated and not tender. She was born at 34 weeks and is otherwise thriving and developing normally, and there are no other similar lesions on her skin.

data_table.Examination: Bright red compressible non ulcerated lesion 22 mm across the left upper eyelid causing mechanical ptosis over the superior half of the pupil when tired, no other cutaneous lesions, no hepatomegaly
data_table.Growth: Weight and length on the 25th centile corrected for gestation, development appropriate for corrected age

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Reassure the parents and review her when she is twelve months old
options.rationale: Watchful waiting is right for the majority of these lesions, which involute over several years without treatment, but a lesion obstructing the visual axis during the critical period of visual development causes deprivation amblyopia and astigmatism from pressure on the globe. Vision lost in the first year is not recovered when the lesion later involutes (Source: RCH CPG: Infantile haemangioma).

options.text: Apply topical timolol gel twice daily and review her in six weeks
options.rationale: Topical beta blocker is effective for thin superficial lesions of a few millimetres depth and is a reasonable choice where there is no functional threat. It penetrates poorly into a 22 mm lesion with a deep component and is too slow for a sight threatening problem (Source: RCH CPG: Infantile haemangioma).

options.text: Refer her for surgical excision of the lesion in the next few weeks
options.rationale: Surgery during the proliferative phase risks significant bleeding and a worse cosmetic outcome than the scar that follows involution, and it is reserved for residual fibrofatty tissue after involution or for lesions that fail medical treatment. Medical treatment shrinks the lesion faster and without a scar (Source: RCH CPG: Infantile haemangioma).

options.text: Refer her for pulsed dye laser treatment over the coming months
options.rationale: Pulsed dye laser penetrates only about a millimetre and is used for ulcerated lesions and for residual telangiectasia after involution, not for a bulky proliferating lesion. It differs from topical treatment mainly in mechanism, sharing the same problem of reaching only the surface (Source: RCH CPG: Infantile haemangioma).

options.text: Refer her urgently for assessment and oral propranolol treatment
options.rationale: Obstruction of the visual axis is one of the accepted indications for systemic treatment, alongside ulceration, airway involvement, disfigurement and high output cardiac failure, and oral propranolol produces measurable shrinkage within days to weeks. It is started after cardiovascular assessment with monitoring of heart rate, blood pressure and blood glucose, ideally before the proliferative phase ends at around five months (Source: RCH CPG: Infantile haemangioma).

explanation.summary: Infantile haemangiomas are usually absent or minimally visible at birth, proliferate rapidly through the first three to five months, plateau, and then involute slowly over several years, which distinguishes them from vascular malformations that are present at birth and grow with the child. Most need no treatment, but a minority require systemic therapy because of their site or complications, and the window for intervention is narrow because treatment works best during proliferation. Indications for oral propranolol are obstruction of vision, the airway or the ear canal, ulceration, high output cardiac failure and lesions likely to cause permanent disfigurement, particularly on the central face. Risk factors include prematurity, low birth weight, female sex and multiple gestation, and five or more cutaneous lesions prompt abdominal ultrasound for hepatic involvement. Segmental facial lesions raise the possibility of PHACE syndrome and warrant cardiac, cerebral and ophthalmological assessment before propranolol is started.
key_points: Proliferation occurs over the first three to five months, so treatment decisions are time critical
Obstruction of the visual axis is an indication for systemic treatment
Oral propranolol is first line, started after cardiovascular assessment
Topical timolol and laser reach only superficial lesions
Five or more cutaneous lesions prompt ultrasound for liver involvement
explanation.pearls: Any periocular haemangioma large enough to touch the eyelid margin needs ophthalmology review even if the pupil looks uncovered, because pressure on the globe induces astigmatism and amblyopia without ever obstructing the visual axis.

sources.label: Australian Medicines Handbook: Children's dosing companion

subtopic_detail: Three years of waxing and waning motor and vocal tics in a boy whose mother is asking for medication after teasing at school
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar seeing an eleven year old boy referred by his general practitioner. For three years he has had bouts of eye blinking, head jerking and shoulder shrugging, and for the past eighteen months he has also cleared his throat and sniffed repeatedly.

His mother says the movements come and go in waves lasting weeks, are worse when he is excited or stressed and almost disappear when he is absorbed in building models. He tells you he feels a build up of pressure behind his eyes before a blink and that he can hold it in during a spelling test but it comes out afterwards in a burst. He also describes needing to touch doorframes an even number of times, and his teacher reports he loses track during long instructions. He has no pain, no injuries from the movements and is achieving at year level, but two boys have started imitating him at lunchtime and he has begun asking to stay home. His mother wants him started on medication today.

data_table.Examination: Frequent eye blinking, head jerking and shoulder shrugging observed during the interview with brief voluntary suppression followed by a burst, intermittent throat clearing, normal neurological examination with no chorea or dystonia
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, urea electrolytes and creatinine, liver function tests, thyroid function and copper studies all within normal limits
data_table.Function: Achieving at year level, no injuries from tics, increasing school avoidance following peer teasing

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Refer him for behavioural therapy for tics with a trained therapist
options.rationale: Comprehensive behavioural intervention for tics, which teaches awareness of the premonitory urge and a competing response, is first line for tics causing distress or impairment and has effect sizes comparable to medication without adverse effects. His clear description of a premonitory urge and of suppressibility indicates he has the awareness the therapy depends on (Source: RANZCP: Tic disorders in children).

options.text: Start risperidone at a low dose and review his tics in four weeks
options.rationale: Antipsychotics reduce tics but carry weight gain, metabolic effects, sedation, hyperprolactinaemia and a small risk of tardive dyskinesia in a child who is achieving at year level and has no injuries. They are reserved for severe or injurious tics that have not responded to behavioural treatment (Source: RANZCP: Tic disorders in children).

options.text: Start clonidine at night and titrate the dose against his tic severity
options.rationale: An alpha 2 agonist is the usual first medication when drug treatment is needed, particularly with coexisting attention problems, and it is better tolerated than an antipsychotic. It still sits after behavioural therapy in the sequence, and sedation and postural hypotension are common (Source: RANZCP: Tic disorders in children).

options.text: Reassure the family that tics resolve by adulthood and take no action
options.rationale: Most tics do improve substantially through adolescence, but he is now avoiding school, which is impairment requiring treatment now rather than a natural history to wait out. Reassurance alone also leaves the coexisting obsessive compulsive and attention symptoms unassessed (Source: RANZCP: Tic disorders in children).

options.text: Refer him for botulinum toxin injections into the affected muscles
options.rationale: Botulinum toxin has a role for a single severe focal motor or vocal tic, such as a painful neck jerk or a loud disruptive vocalisation, and cannot address multiple tics across several muscle groups. It differs from the correct option in being a targeted treatment for a problem he does not have (Source: RANZCP: Tic disorders in children).

explanation.summary: Tourette syndrome requires multiple motor tics and at least one vocal tic present for more than a year with onset before age eighteen, and the tics characteristically wax and wane, shift location over time, worsen with stress or excitement and diminish during absorbing activity. The premonitory urge and brief voluntary suppressibility distinguish tics from chorea, dystonia, myoclonus and seizures, and suppression is typically followed by a rebound burst. Around 85 per cent of children have a coexisting condition, most often attention deficit hyperactivity disorder or obsessive compulsive disorder, and these frequently cause more functional impairment than the tics themselves. Treatment is directed at impairment rather than at tic frequency, and comprehensive behavioural intervention for tics is first line, with alpha 2 agonists and then antipsychotics reserved for tics that remain distressing or injurious. Psychoeducation for the school is a substantial intervention in its own right, since much of the distress comes from peer response rather than from the movements.
key_points: Tourette syndrome needs multiple motor tics plus a vocal tic for over a year with onset before eighteen
A premonitory urge with suppressibility and rebound distinguishes tics from other movements
Coexisting attention and obsessive compulsive symptoms are present in most children
Treatment targets impairment rather than tic frequency
Behavioural therapy is first line, ahead of alpha 2 agonists and antipsychotics
explanation.pearls: Screen every child with tics for obsessive compulsive symptoms and attention difficulties, because in most referred children it is the coexisting condition rather than the tics that is driving the school problem and it responds to a different treatment.

subtopic_detail: Five months of night time hand numbness relieved by shaking, with no wasting and normal thumb abduction strength
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 52 year old bookkeeper with five months of numbness and pins and needles in her right hand. She wakes at around three most mornings with the hand feeling dead and hangs it over the side of the bed and shakes it for a minute or two until the feeling returns.

During the day the symptoms come on when she is holding a book to read or driving, and she has started dropping her coffee cup occasionally. She points to her thumb, index and middle fingers when you ask which part of the hand is affected, and says her little finger is never involved. She has no neck pain and turning or extending her neck does not reproduce the symptoms. On examination sensation is reduced to light touch over the pulps of the first three fingers with normal sensation over the thenar eminence, thumb abduction power is 5 out of 5 and there is no visible thenar wasting. Tapping over the flexor retinaculum reproduces the tingling.

data_table.Examination: Reduced light touch over the pulps of the thumb, index and middle fingers with preserved sensation over the thenar eminence, thumb abduction power 5 out of 5, no thenar wasting, percussion over the flexor retinaculum reproduces tingling, neck movements do not reproduce symptoms
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone, glycated haemoglobin, full blood count and renal function all within normal limits, urine pregnancy test not indicated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Arrange nerve conduction studies before starting any treatment
options.rationale: The clinical picture is characteristic and treatment can begin without electrophysiology, which is reserved for atypical presentations, for confirming the diagnosis before surgery, or where a coexisting neuropathy or radiculopathy is suspected. Waiting for the study delays a simple intervention by weeks (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

options.text: Refer her for urgent surgical decompression of the nerve
options.rationale: Urgent surgery is indicated for constant sensory loss, thenar wasting or weakness of thumb abduction, all of which indicate axonal loss, and she has none of these. Operating on intermittent symptoms without a trial of conservative treatment inverts the accepted sequence (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

options.text: Fit a neutral night wrist splint and review her in six weeks
options.rationale: Nocturnal symptoms arise because the wrist flexes during sleep and raises carpal tunnel pressure, so a splint holding the wrist in neutral overnight is first line for mild to moderate disease and relieves symptoms in the majority within weeks. The intact thumb abduction power and preserved thenar sensation confirm there is no axonal loss requiring more (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

options.text: Arrange an MRI of the cervical spine to look for a radiculopathy
options.rationale: A C6 radiculopathy can produce sensory symptoms in the thumb and index finger but is typically provoked by neck extension and rotation and is accompanied by neck pain and reflex change, none of which is present. Nocturnal symptoms relieved by shaking the hand are not a radicular pattern (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

options.text: Give a corticosteroid injection into the carpal tunnel today
options.rationale: Corticosteroid injection gives short to medium term relief and is a reasonable second step when splinting fails or symptoms are more severe, but it carries a small risk of nerve injury and its benefit commonly wanes over months. It is the next option rather than the first (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

explanation.summary: Carpal tunnel syndrome is the commonest entrapment neuropathy and is diagnosed clinically from nocturnal paraesthesiae in the median nerve distribution relieved by shaking the hand, with symptoms provoked by sustained wrist positions such as driving or holding a book. The single most useful examination finding is preserved sensation over the thenar eminence, because that area is supplied by the palmar cutaneous branch which leaves the nerve proximal to the tunnel, so its involvement points to a more proximal lesion. Secondary causes worth screening for are hypothyroidism, diabetes, pregnancy, rheumatoid arthritis, acromegaly and renal failure. Management is graded, beginning with a neutral night splint and activity modification, then corticosteroid injection, then surgical release, with early surgery for thenar wasting, weakness or constant numbness because those indicate axonal loss that may not recover. Nerve conduction studies are for atypical cases and preoperative confirmation rather than for routine diagnosis.
key_points: Nocturnal paraesthesiae relieved by shaking the hand is the characteristic history
Sparing of sensation over the thenar eminence localises the lesion to the tunnel
Thenar wasting or weak thumb abduction indicates axonal loss and prompts surgical referral
A neutral night splint is first line for mild to moderate disease
Nerve conduction studies are not required for a typical presentation
explanation.pearls: Splint the wrist in neutral rather than in extension, because extension raises carpal tunnel pressure just as flexion does and an off the shelf splint with a metal bar bent backwards is a common reason a correctly indicated splint fails.

sources.label: Australian Rheumatology Association: Carpal tunnel syndrome

subtopic_detail: Four months of bleeding after intercourse with a smooth lesion protruding from the external os and a recent negative screening test
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 34 year old woman who has had light bleeding after intercourse on most occasions over the past four months. She describes it as a smear of fresh blood on wiping afterwards, lasting less than a day.

Her periods are regular every 28 days with no change in flow, and she has no bleeding between periods at any other time. She has taken the combined oral contraceptive pill for six years without missing doses and has had two previous vaginal births. Her last cervical screening test fourteen months ago was negative for human papillomavirus. On speculum examination there is a smooth glistening pedunculated lesion about 12 mm long protruding through the external os on a narrow stalk, which bleeds lightly when touched with a swab. The remainder of the cervix looks healthy with no irregularity, ulceration or friable mass, and there is no abnormal discharge. Tests for chlamydia and gonorrhoea are negative.

data_table.Examination: Smooth glistening pedunculated cervical lesion 12 mm long on a narrow stalk protruding through the external os, bleeding lightly on contact, remaining cervix smooth with no irregularity or ulceration, uterus normal size and mobile, no adnexal masses
data_table.Investigations: Cervical screening test fourteen months ago negative for human papillomavirus, chlamydia and gonorrhoea nucleic acid tests negative, haemoglobin within normal limits, urine pregnancy test negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Repeat her cervical screening test today and manage on the result
options.rationale: A screening test detects human papillomavirus in an asymptomatic population and was negative fourteen months ago, and a negative repeat would not explain the bleeding or remove the lesion. Symptomatic bleeding is investigated on its own merits rather than through the screening program (Source: Cancer Council Australia: National Cervical Screening Program guidelines).
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: National Cervical Screening Program guidelines

options.text: Refer her for colposcopy and take no action at this appointment
options.rationale: Colposcopy is indicated when the cervix looks suspicious with irregularity, ulceration or a friable mass, or where screening is abnormal, and here the surface is smooth with a discrete benign appearing lesion on a stalk. Referral without removing the lesion also leaves the bleeding untreated for months (Source: Cancer Council Australia: National Cervical Screening Program guidelines).
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: National Cervical Screening Program guidelines

options.text: Stop the combined oral contraceptive pill and review her in three months
options.rationale: Hormonal contraception can cause unscheduled bleeding, but that is typically intermenstrual rather than strictly after intercourse, and stopping it does nothing about a visible lesion that bleeds on contact. She would also need alternative contraception for a trial that is unlikely to help (Source: RANZCOG: Abnormal vaginal bleeding).

options.text: Remove the polyp in clinic and send it for histological examination
options.rationale: A pedunculated polyp on a narrow stalk that bleeds on contact explains her postcoital bleeding and can be avulsed in clinic by grasping the stalk with sponge forceps and twisting, which is both diagnostic and curative. Histology is mandatory because a small proportion harbour dysplasia or malignancy despite a benign appearance (Source: RANZCOG: Abnormal vaginal bleeding).

options.text: Refer her for hysteroscopy and endometrial sampling under anaesthetic
options.rationale: Endometrial assessment is directed at intermenstrual or postmenopausal bleeding and at risk factors for endometrial pathology, and she has regular cycles with bleeding only after intercourse. Hysteroscopy has a role where a polyp appears to arise from the endocervical canal or where symptoms persist after removal (Source: RANZCOG: Abnormal vaginal bleeding).

explanation.summary: Postcoital bleeding is caused most often by cervical ectropion, cervical polyps, cervicitis from chlamydia or gonorrhoea, or vaginal atrophy, but cervical cancer must be excluded in every case because it is the diagnosis that cannot wait. The critical principle is that a negative human papillomavirus screening result does not exclude cancer in a symptomatic woman, since a small proportion of cervical cancers are not associated with the virus and false negatives occur, so the appearance of the cervix drives the decision. A visibly abnormal, irregular, ulcerated or friable cervix is referred for colposcopy and biopsy regardless of the screening result, whereas a discrete benign appearing polyp on a stalk can be removed in clinic. All removed tissue goes for histology. Persistent postcoital bleeding after treatment of an apparent cause is itself an indication for specialist referral rather than reassurance.
key_points: A negative human papillomavirus test does not exclude cancer in a symptomatic woman
The appearance of the cervix determines whether colposcopy is needed
A pedunculated polyp on a narrow stalk can be avulsed in clinic
All removed cervical tissue is sent for histological examination
Test for chlamydia and gonorrhoea in every case of postcoital bleeding
explanation.pearls: Postcoital bleeding that persists after an apparent cause has been treated warrants specialist referral even with negative screening and normal histology, because that pattern is how the small number of screen negative cervical cancers are eventually found.

sources.label: Cancer Council Australia: National Cervical Screening Program guidelines

subtopic_detail: A head circumference crossing from the 50th to above the 97th centile over three months with a tense fontanelle and vomiting
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a five month old boy brought by his parents because he has become increasingly unsettled and has vomited most mornings for the past fortnight.

His head circumference was on the 50th centile at his six week check and at his three month check, and today it measures above the 97th centile. His parents say he used to hold his head up steadily and reach for toys, and that over the past month he has stopped doing both. On examination his anterior fontanelle is full and tense while he is sitting quietly upright, the scalp veins are prominent, and when you sit him up his eyes deviate downward so that white sclera is visible above the iris. He was born at term with an uncomplicated delivery. His father's head circumference is on the 50th centile for an adult man. There is no bruising anywhere on his body and an ophthalmologist has examined his retinae this afternoon and found no haemorrhages.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 132 per minute, blood pressure 88/52 mmHg, respiratory rate 34 per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Anterior fontanelle full and tense while upright and settled, prominent scalp veins, downward deviation of the eyes with sclera visible above the iris on sitting, loss of previously acquired head control and reaching, no bruising, retinae free of haemorrhage on ophthalmological examination
data_table.Growth: Head circumference on the 50th centile at six weeks and three months, above the 97th centile today, weight and length on the 50th centile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Reassure the parents this is benign familial macrocephaly and review in a month
options.rationale: Benign familial macrocephaly runs along a large but parallel centile line in a well infant with a large parent, whereas this head has crossed three centile lines in three months in a child with a tense fontanelle, vomiting and lost skills. His father's head circumference on the 50th centile removes the familial explanation entirely (Source: RCH CPG: Macrocephaly).

options.text: Arrange urgent neuroimaging and discuss him with a neurosurgical service
options.rationale: Rapid centile crossing with a tense fontanelle when upright, distended scalp veins, downward eye deviation and developmental regression is progressive raised intracranial pressure, and imaging with immediate neurosurgical involvement is required because untreated hydrocephalus causes irreversible visual and cognitive loss. Cranial ultrasound through the open fontanelle can be obtained within minutes as the first study while the referral is made (Source: RCH CPG: Macrocephaly).

options.text: Arrange a skeletal survey and notify child protection before imaging his head
options.rationale: Abusive head trauma is an important cause of rapid head growth in infancy, but it is argued against here by the absence of bruising and of retinal haemorrhages, and by the gradual centile crossing with preserved growth elsewhere. Investigating that possibility first would delay imaging in a child with active signs of raised pressure (Source: RCH CPG: Macrocephaly).

options.text: Request an outpatient MRI of the brain at the next available appointment
options.rationale: Magnetic resonance imaging gives the best anatomical detail and will be needed, but obtaining it as an outpatient in an infant who requires sedation takes weeks, and the pressure is rising now. It differs from the correct option only in timing, and timing is the whole question (Source: RCH CPG: Macrocephaly).

options.text: Measure his head circumference again in four weeks and plot the trajectory
options.rationale: Serial measurement is the right approach to isolated macrocephaly in a thriving infant with a soft fontanelle and normal development, none of which describes this child. Another four weeks of untreated raised pressure risks permanent optic atrophy (Source: RCH CPG: Macrocephaly).

explanation.summary: Head circumference is plotted at every infant health check precisely so that a change in trajectory is detected before the clinical signs of raised pressure appear, and crossing centile lines is far more significant than any single large measurement. Benign familial macrocephaly and benign enlargement of the subarachnoid spaces are the common benign causes and both feature a well infant with normal development, a soft fontanelle and growth along a parallel line, usually with a large parent. The findings that indicate raised intracranial pressure in an infant are a tense fontanelle when upright and settled, distended scalp veins, sunsetting eyes from pressure on the dorsal midbrain, irritability, vomiting, developmental regression and a high pitched cry. Causes include obstructive and communicating hydrocephalus, intracranial mass, chronic subdural collections including from abusive head trauma, and venous sinus thrombosis. Cranial ultrasound through the anterior fontanelle is the fastest first study in an infant, with computed tomography or magnetic resonance imaging following as directed by the neurosurgical team.
key_points: Crossing head circumference centiles matters more than a single large measurement
A tense fontanelle when upright and settled indicates raised pressure
Sunsetting eyes reflect pressure on the dorsal midbrain
Loss of previously acquired skills is regression and is never benign
Cranial ultrasound through the open fontanelle is the fastest first investigation
explanation.pearls: Always plot the parents' head circumferences before accepting benign familial macrocephaly, since the diagnosis requires a large parent as well as a well infant, and a normal sized parent converts a reassuring measurement into one that needs explaining.

sources.label: Royal Children's Hospital: Raised intracranial pressure
